question: What dropout rate was applied to the sums of the embeddings and the positional encodings in the Transformer?
ground_truth: A dropout rate of P_drop = 0.1 was applied to the sums of the embeddings and the positional encodings in both the encoder and decoder stacks.
target_citation: [Attention Is All You Need, Residual Dropout, Page 8]
verified_quote: In addition, we apply dropout to the sums of the embeddings and the positional encodings in both the encoder and decoder stacks. For the base model, we use a rate of P drop = 0 . 1 .

question: How many warmup steps were used in the Adam optimizer learning rate schedule?
ground_truth: warmup_steps = 4000 were used in the Adam optimizer learning rate schedule.
target_citation: [Attention Is All You Need, 5.3 Optimizer, Page 7]

question: What was the value of the label smoothing parameter used during training?
ground_truth: During training, label smoothing of value epsilon_ls = 0.1 was employed.
target_citation: [Attention Is All You Need, Label Smoothing, Page 8]
verified_quote: During training, we employed label smoothing of value ϵ ls = 0 . 1 [ 36 ]. This hurts perplexity, as the model learns to be more unsure, but improves accuracy and BLEU score.

question: What were the dimension sizes for keys (d_k) and values (d_v) in each head of the 8-head multi-head attention?
ground_truth: For each of the h = 8 parallel attention heads, d_k = d_v = d_model / h = 64.
target_citation: [Attention Is All You Need, 3.2.2 Multi-Head Attention, Page 5]
verified_quote: In this work we employ h = 8 parallel attention layers, or heads. For each of these we use d k = d v = d model /h = 64 .

question: What is the bitrate and frame rate of the Mimi neural audio codec used in Moshi?
ground_truth: The Mimi codec operates at a frame rate of 12.5 Hz (corresponding to an 80ms stride) and a bitrate of 1.1 kbps.
target_citation: [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, 3.3.1 Architecture, Page 11]
verified_quote: We use Q = 8 quantizers, each with a codebook size of N A = 2048. At 12.5Hz, this represents a bitrate of 1.1kbps.

question: How does the acoustic delay relate to the audio frame step size in Moshi, and what latency does it introduce?
ground_truth: Each step of acoustic delay corresponds to 1 audio frame (80 ms step size). Pretraining uses an acoustic delay of 2 steps (160 ms), fine-tuning uses an acoustic delay of 1 step (80 ms), and practical conversational latency is approximately 200 ms.
target_citation: [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, 5.3 Ablations on generative modeling, Page 26]
verified_quote: Moreover, and as described in Table 1 , we settle on a theoretical latency of 160ms by pretraining Moshi with an acoustic delay of 2 and finetuning it with an acoustic delay of 1.

question: How many Residual Vector Quantization (RVQ) codebooks does the Mimi codec utilize for speech, and what is the codebook size?
ground_truth: Mimi uses Q = 8 RVQ codebooks (quantizers), each with a codebook size of N_A = 2048 centroids.
target_citation: [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, 3.3.1 Architecture, Page 11]
verified_quote: We use Q = 8 quantizers, each with a codebook size of N A = 2048.

question: What is the overall latency claimed for Moshi in conversational dialogue (both theoretical and practical)?
ground_truth: Moshi achieves a theoretical latency of 160 ms and approximately 200 ms in practice.
target_citation: [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, Abstract, Page 1]
verified_quote: Our resulting model is the first real-time full-duplex spoken large language model, with a theoretical latency of 160ms, 200ms in practice, and is available at github.com/kyutai-labs/moshi .

question: What was the data efficiency gain observed for H-Net on DNA sequences compared to baseline models?
ground_truth: H-Net demonstrated nearly a 4x improvement in data efficiency over baselines on DNA sequences (specifically 3.6x compared to isotropic models).
target_citation: [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, Abstract, Page 1]
verified_quote: or DNA sequences (nearly 4 × improvement in data efficiency over baselines), showing the potential of true end-to-end models that learn and scale better from unprocessed data.

question: How does H-Net dynamically determine chunk boundaries without a tokenizer?
ground_truth: H-Net uses a chunking layer with a routing module that calculates cosine similarity between adjacent encoder outputs to predict boundary probabilities p_t and discrete boundary indicators b_t directly from raw data.
target_citation: [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, 2.2.1 Chunking Layer, Page 6]
verified_quote: The routing module implements this intuition through cosine similarity between adjacent encoder outputs.

question: What sequence modalities were tested to evaluate H-Net beyond standard English text?
ground_truth: Chinese text, computer source code, and DNA sequences.
target_citation: [Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling, 3.2 Alternate Language Datasets, Page 15]
verified_quote: Besides conventional language modeling, we also examine three other language modeling settings: Chinese, code, and DNA.

question: What is the dynamic chunk size and frame rate used for streaming speech tokens in H-Net?
ground_truth: REFUSAL: The paper on H-Net (Dynamic Chunking) does not model streaming speech; frame rates and streaming speech tokens belong to the Moshi paper, not H-Net.

question: How does the Transformer encoder in Attention Is All You Need dynamically adjust chunk boundaries for self-attention?
ground_truth: REFUSAL: Attention Is All You Need does not dynamically adjust chunk boundaries; dynamic chunking is introduced in the H-Net paper, whereas the 2017 Transformer uses static full-sequence self-attention.
